entry.title: Zakura's sendrawtransaction Retry Channel Can Be Poisoned by Invalid Transactions
entry.content:
Zakura 1.2.0 admits a deserializable transaction into a retry channel before full mempool validation completes. A transaction that later fails consensus or mempool checks can therefore consume retry-channel capacity and downstream processing time even though the RPC ultimately rejects it.

The channel has a shared capacity of only 20 entries. A caller who can submit enough deserializable but invalid transactions can fill that capacity, create retry lag, and delay legitimate temporary retries. The strongest established consequence is wasted retry work and channel pressure. The reviewed evidence does not by itself prove that a valid transaction is permanently evicted or loses relay end to end.

Vulnerability at a glance

The report identifies the affected product and version as:

  • Product: Zakura / zakurad
  • Version: 1.2.0
  • Status: published
  • Weakness classes: CWE-770, allocation of resources without limits or throttling; and CWE-400, uncontrolled resource consumption

The attack requires access to sendrawtransaction, a submitted payload that can be deserialized but fails later validation, and enough requests to fill or overrun the 20-item retry channel. In the default RPC deployment, a privileged cookie is required, so RPC exposure and authentication policy directly affect the attacker population.

The ordering flaw

The relevant ordering is:

Deserialization proves only that the bytes can be represented as a transaction object. It does not prove that the transaction is valid for consensus, acceptable to the mempool, or worth retrying.

Because the queue operation runs first, a transaction can enter the retry consumer before the later mempool call returns. When validation fails permanently, the RPC caller receives an error, but the earlier queue admission is not necessarily retracted.

The intended behavior is narrower: only a transaction with a legitimate temporary failure should enter retry state. A permanent consensus or policy failure should be discarded immediately.

How the channel becomes poisoned

The retry path can be pressured as follows:

  1. Submit a transaction that passes deserialization but is invalid during full validation.
  2. Let sendrawtransaction enqueue it before the mempool result is known.
  3. Repeat until the shared channel approaches its capacity of 20.
  4. Allow the retry worker to process entries that can never succeed.
  5. Observe channel lag and delayed handling of legitimate temporary retries.

The attack is not a crash primitive by itself. The resource being consumed is retry work and channel capacity. Its effect is to make the retry system spend time on entries that should never have been admitted.

Why a capacity of 20 matters

The channel is deliberately small:

A bounded channel prevents unbounded memory growth, but a small shared queue also means a modest burst can create visible pressure. Once downstream structures reach capacity, oldest-entry removal may discard work without distinguishing attacker-generated permanent failures from legitimate temporary retries.

Bounded memory is useful, but it is not sufficient queue hygiene. The system must also ensure that only retryable work enters the queue.

Normal and abnormal behavior

In the normal case, a transaction that needs a legitimate temporary retry condition enters the retry structure, while permanent validation failures are discarded immediately.

In the abnormal case, the transaction occupies retry work before validation completes. The later RPC error does not undo the earlier enqueue, so invalid entries remain capable of consuming retry processing and channel capacity.

The distinction between temporary and permanent failure is important:

  • temporary network or synchronization conditions may justify retrying;
  • a consensus-invalid transaction cannot become valid by being retried;
  • a permanent mempool policy rejection should not occupy the retry consumer; and
  • malformed input that cannot be deserialized should never reach the channel.

Impact and evidence boundary

The established impact includes:

  • invalid transactions consuming retry-channel capacity;
  • repeated validation work for submissions that cannot succeed;
  • retry lag that can delay legitimate temporary work; and
  • a larger abuse surface when RPC is exposed without authentication.

The report carefully limits a stronger claim. Channel lag alone does not prove that the downstream IndexMap became full or that a valid transaction was permanently lost. Demonstrating final eviction or relay loss requires a controlled end-to-end comparison with a valid transaction and a complete observation of the retry and mempool outcomes.

This distinction matters operationally. The issue is already a resource-consumption problem even if every legitimate transaction eventually recovers.

Safe validation approach

Testing should use an isolated node and a bounded set of deserializable but consensus-invalid transactions. Submit enough requests to observe RPC rejection, retry-channel lag, and downstream queue metrics. Then run a separate controlled valid-temporary-retry case before making claims about final eviction.

A conceptual test sequence is:

The test must not target production nodes or attempt uncontrolled queue flooding. Metrics should distinguish channel occupancy, failure class, retry attempts, evictions, and successful completion.

Remediation

The primary fix is to move retry admission after full validation, or to enqueue only failures explicitly classified as temporary:

Permanent consensus failures must never be retried. A failure-aware eviction policy should also distinguish temporary retry work from entries that repeatedly fail permanently.

Additional safeguards should include:

  • per-caller or per-authenticated-principal quotas for retry-generating requests;
  • bounded retry attempts and backoff for temporary failures;
  • separate queues or metrics for validation, retry, and final eviction;
  • explicit classification of failure types before queue admission; and
  • RPC source restrictions and request-rate limits while queue semantics are being corrected.

Regression tests

The fix should include tests that:

  1. Verify that a permanent validation failure never enters the retry consumer.
  2. Fill the channel with invalid submissions and confirm that legitimate temporary retry work remains represented.
  3. Confirm that retry metrics distinguish channel lag from downstream eviction and final transaction outcome.
  4. Compare default cookie-authenticated RPC with an explicitly exposed configuration.
  5. Verify that retry attempts are bounded and permanent failures do not re-enter the queue.
  6. Confirm that a valid transaction completes normally after invalid submission pressure is released.

Takeaway

A retry queue is only as safe as its admission policy. Bounded capacity limits memory growth, but it does not prevent denial of service when permanently failing work is admitted before the system knows whether it is retryable.

For Zakura operators, keep RPC authenticated and restrict its source network while this path is being hardened. For maintainers, validate first, classify failure second, and enqueue only work that has a credible chance of succeeding later. The strongest current conclusion is retry-channel pressure and wasted work; claims of permanent valid-transaction loss require a separate end-to-end proof.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-sendrawtransaction-retry-channel-poisoning/report.pdf

entry.title: Zakura Broadcast Gateway Can Be Hijacked Through a Plaintext Backend Relay
entry.content:
Zakura 1.2.0 has a broadcast-gateway trust-boundary problem when it forwards transactions to a remote backend over unauthenticated plaintext HTTP. The client may submit sendrawtransaction over HTTPS to the gateway, but the next network hop can still expose and alter the transaction.

The gateway also treats a successful HTTP status as sufficient evidence that broadcasting succeeded. An on-path attacker can return an arbitrary HTTP 200 response containing a fabricated transaction ID, causing the gateway and its client to believe that the transaction was accepted even though no real node received it.

This is a relay-hijacking and response-authenticity issue. It can expose transaction contents, suppress or replace broadcasts, and create false success signals for wallets or automation.

Vulnerability at a glance

The report identifies the affected product and version as:

  • Product: Zakura / zakurad
  • Version: 1.2.0
  • Status: published
  • Weakness classes: CWE-319, cleartext transmission of sensitive information; and CWE-345, insufficient verification of data authenticity

The issue is triggered when at least one configured gateway backend uses a non-loopback plaintext URL such as:

An attacker must control, observe, redirect, or inject traffic on the gateway-to-backend path. The client-facing HTTPS connection does not remove this risk because it protects only the client-to-gateway leg.

The trust boundary that fails

A secure deployment should authenticate both ends of every cross-host hop. In the normal flow:

  1. A wallet or broadcast client submits a transaction to the gateway over HTTPS.
  2. The gateway forwards the JSON-RPC request to a backend node.
  3. The backend authenticates the gateway and proves the integrity of the response.
  4. The gateway validates the JSON-RPC envelope and transaction ID.
  5. The gateway fails over if the backend response is invalid or unavailable.

The vulnerable flow replaces the third and fourth steps with an unauthenticated HTTP request and a status-code check:

The gateway therefore authenticates the client-facing connection but does not authenticate the server on the next hop. HTTPS on the first leg cannot provide end-to-end integrity for the second leg.

Why HTTP 200 is not proof of success

HTTP status describes the transport-level response, not the semantic result of the JSON-RPC method. A backend can return HTTP 200 with:

  • a JSON-RPC error object;
  • the wrong request ID;
  • a malformed result;
  • an invalid transaction ID; or
  • a fabricated but syntactically plausible transaction ID.

If the gateway accepts any response with a status below 500, an attacker can forge a success without running a node or validating the submitted transaction:

The result is a false acknowledgment. The client may display a successful broadcast or stop retrying, while the transaction never enters a real mempool.

What an attacker can do

An on-path attacker with visibility into the gateway-to-backend route may:

  • read transaction contents sent to a remote backend;
  • drop valid broadcasts so they never reach a node;
  • alter or replace request traffic;
  • inject an HTTP 200 response with a fabricated 64-character transaction ID; and
  • prevent failover by making the gateway believe the first backend succeeded.

The attacker does not need to compromise the client-facing HTTPS connection. The required position is on the separate backend route, such as an exposed cross-host network, an untrusted segment, or an improperly secured VPN path.

Factors that increase the risk

The risk is higher when:

  • repository or deployment configuration contains cross-host http:// backend URLs;
  • the backend is not restricted to loopback or a trusted private network;
  • requests carry no RPC cookie, gateway token, or client identity;
  • the connection does not use TLS or mutual TLS; and
  • the gateway treats HTTP 200 as success without validating JSON-RPC semantics.

A forged 200 response is particularly damaging because it blocks normal failover. A healthy secondary backend may never be called if the gateway considers the attacker’s response valid.

Safe validation approach

Testing should use an isolated gateway and controlled backend. Point the first backend at a test server that returns HTTP 200 with either a fake transaction ID or a JSON-RPC error. Then verify whether the gateway relays the body, reports failure, and calls a known healthy secondary backend.

A representative controlled response is:

The test should confirm that an invalid or unexpected transaction ID is never reported as a successful broadcast. It should not be run against production nodes or real transaction traffic.

Remediation

Every cross-host backend connection should use one of the following:

  • mutually authenticated TLS;
  • a trusted VPN with authenticated tunnel endpoints; or
  • an authenticated and integrity-protected private transport.

The gateway should reject non-loopback plaintext HTTP backends during configuration loading unless an explicit secure tunnel profile is enabled. This turns a dangerous deployment choice into a visible startup failure instead of a silent trust-boundary downgrade.

Response validation must be semantic, not just transport-level. For sendrawtransaction, the gateway should validate:

  • the complete JSON-RPC envelope;
  • the response id matches the request;
  • no JSON-RPC error field is present;
  • the result has the expected transaction ID type and exact 64-hex-character format; and
  • the response corresponds to the submitted request and backend identity.

Any semantic validation failure should trigger backend failure handling and failover, just as a transport exception or 5xx response would.

Regression tests

The fix should include tests that:

  1. Reject a non-loopback http:// backend unless an explicit secure tunnel profile is active.
  2. Return HTTP 200 with a JSON-RPC error and verify that the gateway fails over.
  3. Return HTTP 200 with malformed JSON, the wrong request ID, or an invalid transaction ID and verify failure.
  4. Return HTTP 200 with a fabricated valid-looking transaction ID and verify that it is not treated as broadcast success.
  5. Verify that backend certificate and client-identity failures are reported and never converted into success.
  6. Confirm that a valid authenticated backend response still completes the normal broadcast flow.

Takeaway

TLS is only meaningful when it covers the entire path that needs integrity and peer authentication. Protecting the client-to-gateway connection while sending the gateway-to-backend request over plaintext leaves the most important relay decision exposed.

For Zakura operators, remote backends should use mutually authenticated TLS or a genuinely authenticated private tunnel, and plaintext cross-host URLs should be removed. For maintainers, the gateway must validate JSON-RPC semantics and transaction identity rather than treating HTTP 200 as proof that a transaction was accepted.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-broadcast-gateway-relay-hijacking/report.pdf

entry.title: How Zakura 1.2.0 Bounds Indexer gRPC Resource Exhaustion
entry.content:
Zakura’s indexer gRPC service historically presented an unauthenticated resource-exhaustion surface. A remotely reachable plaintext endpoint could retain long-lived connections and streaming state with weak global limits, allowing anonymous clients to compete with legitimate indexer users.

The important result of the reviewed report is that Zakura 1.2.0 closes the tested unbounded-growth path. It introduces hard ceilings for retained connections and concurrent HTTP/2 streams, together with a TLS handshake timeout. This should therefore be read as a fix-verification and configuration-hardening record, not as evidence that version 1.2.0 remains vulnerable to unbounded connection growth.

Network access control is still necessary. A bounded service can resist uncontrolled growth while remaining susceptible to quota saturation if an anonymous client is allowed to consume the entire configured budget.

Scope and deployment conditions

The indexer gRPC service exists only when the indexer feature is built and indexer_listen_addr is configured. The historical risk requires the endpoint to be reachable by an untrusted client that attempts many TCP connections, concurrent HTTP/2 streams, long-lived subscriptions, or stalled TLS handshakes.

The report classifies the historical weaknesses as:

  • CWE-306: missing authentication for a critical function;
  • CWE-770: allocation of resources without limits or throttling.

Binding the service to loopback or placing it behind a private authenticated gateway prevents direct anonymous Internet access. This remains the recommended deployment posture even with the 1.2.0 limits enabled.

Why streaming endpoints need several limits

One rate or connection limit is not enough for gRPC. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, subscriptions can remain active for a long time, and TLS negotiation consumes resources before an RPC begins.

A complete resource boundary therefore needs to govern at least three layers:

  1. Total retained TCP connections.
  2. Concurrent HTTP/2 streams on each connection.
  3. Time spent waiting for an incomplete TLS handshake.

If any layer is unbounded, an attacker can shift pressure to it. A connection cap without a stream cap permits stream multiplication. A stream cap without a connection cap permits connection multiplication. Both controls can still be occupied indefinitely if silent TLS handshakes never expire.

The 1.2.0 connection boundary

Zakura 1.2.0 uses a global semaphore to gate accepted connections before they retain long-lived service state. The reviewed limit is 64 connections:

The permit remains associated with the connection and is released when that work ends. As a result, additional clients cannot create unlimited retained service state once all 64 permits are occupied.

This is stronger than merely counting connection arrivals. It measures active retained work, which is the resource that matters for long-lived gRPC subscriptions.

The HTTP/2 stream boundary

Each connection also has a concurrent-stream ceiling of 64. The Tonic service configuration and the underlying HTTP/2 configuration use the same value:

Synchronizing these settings prevents a client from bypassing an application-level limit through lower-level HTTP/2 behavior. A single connection can still use its full allocation, but it cannot create an unbounded number of simultaneous subscription streams.

The TLS handshake boundary

The TLS path applies a ten-second timeout:

This prevents a silent peer from retaining a connection slot forever without completing TLS. It closes the pre-request waiting pattern in which a client connects, sends no useful handshake data, and leaves server resources allocated indefinitely.

Together, the three controls produce a bounded call chain:

What risk remains

Hard ceilings prevent unlimited growth, but they do not authenticate clients. A plaintext endpoint exposed to an untrusted network can still reveal its methods through gRPC reflection and allow anonymous callers to consume the full configured quota. Long-lived subscriptions retain application and HTTP/2 state until they end or expire.

The likely result is bounded quota saturation rather than host-wide unbounded exhaustion. Legitimate indexer users may still be delayed or rejected while an attacker occupies available connections and streams. The streamed chain-tip and mempool information is primarily public data, so availability is the main concern described by the report.

Configuration changes can also reintroduce the original risk. Raising limits without capacity analysis, removing the semaphore, desynchronizing HTTP/2 and application stream caps, or disabling the handshake timeout would weaken the verified boundary.

Safe verification

Validation should use an isolated Zakura 1.2.0 node. The test should attempt slightly more than each documented limit rather than trying to exhaust the host:

A legitimate ChainTipChange subscription should remain usable below the boundary and recover after test connections are released. Operators should monitor rejected connections, stream saturation, handshake timeouts, active subscriptions, and permit usage so quota pressure is visible before it affects users.

Hardening recommendations

The 1.2.0 limits should be treated as non-optional security invariants. They should not be removed or made arbitrarily configurable without equivalent safeguards and capacity checks.

Deployment and maintenance controls should include:

  • place externally reachable gRPC behind TLS and authenticated access control;
  • bind directly exposed indexer services to loopback or trusted private networks;
  • restrict or disable gRPC reflection outside debugging and management environments;
  • keep connection, stream, and handshake limits synchronized and documented;
  • expose saturation and quota-rejection metrics; and
  • alert when anonymous or unexpected clients approach the configured ceilings.

Authentication and limits serve different purposes. Authentication restricts who may consume resources, while hard limits cap the damage if credentials, network policy, or gateway configuration fail.

Regression tests

The verified behavior should be protected by tests that:

  1. Open 65 retained connections and confirm that the extra connection waits or is rejected without retaining additional service state.
  2. Attempt 65 concurrent streams on one connection and verify the documented per-connection cap.
  3. Hold a TLS handshake silent and verify expiration near ten seconds.
  4. Confirm that a legitimate ChainTipChange call succeeds below the limit.
  5. Release test connections and verify that permits and stream capacity return promptly.
  6. Confirm that plaintext and reflection exposure match the documented deployment policy.

Takeaway

Zakura 1.2.0 demonstrates the right shape of defense for a streaming RPC service: bound connections, bound streams, and bound pre-authentication handshake time. The reviewed implementation prevents the historical unbounded-growth path under the tested design.

That does not make an anonymously exposed gRPC endpoint a good deployment choice. Operators should retain the 1.2.0 resource ceilings and add TLS, authentication, private-network binding, reflection restrictions, and quota monitoring. Bounded anonymous access is safer than unbounded anonymous access, but authenticated bounded access is the stronger security boundary.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-indexer-grpc-resource-boundaries/report.pdf

entry.title: Zakura's Health Endpoint Is Vulnerable to Slowloris Resource Exhaustion
entry.content:
Zakura 1.2.0 includes a rate limit for its health endpoint, but that control only limits how quickly new connections are accepted. It does not limit how long accepted connections remain alive or how many connection tasks can exist at once.

This distinction creates a Slowloris-style denial-of-service risk. An unauthenticated client can open incomplete or persistent HTTP connections at a rate below the configured threshold and keep them alive across multiple rate-limit windows. Sockets and tasks accumulate until file descriptors are exhausted, legitimate health checks fail, and other node services may lose access to process-wide resources.

Vulnerability at a glance

The report identifies the affected product and version as:

  • Product: Zakura / zakurad
  • Version: 1.2.0
  • Status: published
  • Weakness classes: CWE-400, uncontrolled resource consumption, and CWE-770, allocation of resources without limits or throttling

The endpoint is disabled unless health.listen_addr is configured, so default deployments without the health listener are not exposed. Risk appears when the listener is enabled on an address reachable by untrusted clients and no reverse proxy or operating-system policy imposes a stricter connection lifetime or active-connection cap.

Why the existing rate limit is insufficient

The server waits for its rate limiter before accepting a new connection and then spawns a task to serve it:

This bounds arrivals during each time window, but accepted connections are no longer represented in the limiter’s decision. If an attacker opens connections slowly enough to remain below the threshold, every new window admits additional connections while the older ones remain active.

Arrival rate and retained work are different resources. A robust listener needs controls for both.

The attack path

The health endpoint has no authentication by design once it is reachable. An attacker can exploit it without credentials:

  1. Connect to the configured health port.
  2. Send an incomplete HTTP header or hold a keep-alive connection open.
  3. Keep the connection below any idle or protocol-level closure condition.
  4. Open more connections slowly enough to remain under the arrival-rate threshold.
  5. Repeat across multiple rate-limit windows.
  6. Accumulate sockets and connection tasks until the process reaches its file-descriptor limit.

Normal health clients send a small complete request, receive a response, and release the connection within a short bounded lifetime. The malicious behavior is deliberately incomplete: the client sends partial headers or keeps the connection alive so the server retains a socket and task indefinitely.

The call chain looks like this:

Three root causes

1. The limiter controls arrivals, not concurrency

A fixed-window rate limiter answers how many connections may arrive during a period. It does not answer how many accepted connections are still active. A low-rate attacker can therefore remain compliant with the limit while steadily increasing retained work.

2. Connection lifetime is unbounded

The listener does not enforce sufficiently short header, idle, keep-alive, or total connection deadlines. It also lacks a global semaphore limiting active serve_connection tasks. Partial requests can remain pending while new tasks continue to be admitted.

3. Accept errors can amplify the outage

The accept loop logs an error and immediately retries:

After file-descriptor exhaustion, repeated EMFILE errors can create a hot loop. CPU use and warning-log volume then rise at the same time that the health endpoint is already unavailable, expanding a socket-exhaustion problem into an additional processing and disk-I/O problem.

Security impact

The primary impact is availability loss. Legitimate readiness and liveness probes can fail, causing load balancers or orchestration systems to mark the node unhealthy, remove it from service, or restart it. Because file descriptors are shared across the process, exhaustion can also interfere with peer, RPC, and other node sockets.

The report does not establish data disclosure or transaction modification. Exposure is also reduced when the endpoint is bound to loopback or an internal-only management network. A reverse proxy that enforces header, idle, lifetime, and concurrent-connection limits can provide immediate protection.

Health endpoints deserve particular care because production platforms often expose them to cluster and load-balancer networks. Those networks are not necessarily equivalent to a fully trusted process boundary.

Safe validation approach

Validation should take place only in an isolated environment. Open a bounded set of incomplete HTTP connections at a rate below the configured threshold, hold them across several rate windows, and monitor whether active connections continue to grow. Then check whether a normal /healthy request still completes.

A minimal test connection can send a partial request and deliberately omit the final header terminator:

The test should remain bounded and stop well before host-level exhaustion. The goal is to verify timeout and concurrency behavior, not to reproduce a production outage.

Remediation

The health listener needs limits on retained work in addition to its arrival-rate limit:

  • enforce short header, idle, keep-alive, and total connection timeouts;
  • acquire a global semaphore permit before spawning each connection task;
  • add optional per-source connection quotas;
  • combine arrival-rate controls with active-connection and lifetime limits;
  • apply bounded backoff to repeated accept errors; and
  • default the endpoint to loopback or an internal management network.

An external reverse proxy can provide a useful near-term boundary, but application-level controls are still important. Direct exposure, proxy bypass, or proxy configuration drift should not restore an unlimited connection lifetime.

Regression tests

The fix should be covered by tests that verify:

  1. A partial request is closed after each configured timeout.
  2. Connections opened below the arrival limit across multiple windows cannot exceed the active cap.
  3. A valid /healthy request remains responsive at the configured safe-load boundary.
  4. Keep-alive sessions cannot exceed their idle or total lifetime.
  5. Forced accept errors trigger bounded backoff without a CPU or warning-log hot loop.
  6. Connection permits are released after normal completion, timeout, and client disconnect.

Takeaway

Rate limiting is not the same as resource limiting. A server can accept connections slowly and still accumulate an unbounded amount of retained work when connection lifetimes are uncontrolled.

For Zakura operators, the immediate defense is to keep the health endpoint on loopback or an internal network and place a tightly configured reverse proxy in front of any remotely reachable listener. For maintainers, the durable repair is a combination of request deadlines, an active-connection semaphore, per-source quotas, and resilient accept-error handling.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-health-endpoint-slowloris/report.pdf

entry.title: Silent TLS Handshakes Can Exhaust Zakura RPC Connections
entry.content:
Zakura 1.2.0 has a pre-authentication denial-of-service risk in its TLS-enabled RPC listener. The server accepts a TCP connection, immediately creates an asynchronous task, and waits for the TLS handshake without a deadline or a global connection limit.

An anonymous remote client can exploit that behavior simply by opening TCP connections and remaining silent. Each connection retains a socket, a task, and TLS state before RPC authentication is reached. Enough pending connections can exhaust file descriptors or task capacity, prevent legitimate RPC clients from connecting, and potentially cause the RPC service or node to exit.

Vulnerability at a glance

The report identifies the affected product and version as:

  • Product: Zakura / zakurad
  • Version: 1.2.0
  • Status: published
  • Weakness classes: CWE-400, uncontrolled resource consumption, and CWE-770, allocation of resources without limits or throttling

The attack requires a deployment with rpc.tls enabled and a TLS RPC listener reachable by the attacker. No RPC cookie or valid client certificate is required unless an external front layer enforces one before admitting the TCP connection.

The practical trigger conditions are straightforward:

  1. TLS RPC is enabled and reachable.
  2. The attacker can establish TCP connections.
  3. The attacker does not complete the TLS handshake.
  4. Connections arrive faster than the operating system or application releases resources.
  5. No firewall, proxy, or TLS terminator enforces a lower connection and handshake budget.

Why authentication does not help

The vulnerable work happens before RPC authentication. A normal client completes TLS within a short period, reaches authentication, processes a request, and releases its connection resources when the session ends.

A malicious client stops earlier. It connects but sends no ClientHello, or sends only part of the handshake. Because the TLS future has no timeout, the socket and its task can remain pending indefinitely. Cookie authentication never runs, so valid credentials are irrelevant to the attacker.

Rate limiting completed RPC requests also misses the problem. The retained resources belong to connections that have not yet become RPC requests.

The vulnerable call chain

The listener accepts connections in a loop and creates a new Tokio task for each socket:

This structure has no permit acquisition before tokio::spawn, and acceptor.accept(socket).await has no handshake deadline. The resulting path is:

If accept() begins returning EMFILE because the process has exhausted its file-descriptor allowance, the RPC task can terminate. Depending on error propagation and service supervision, that failure can contribute to full node shutdown rather than a temporary refusal of excess clients.

Three root causes

1. Unbounded task creation

Every accepted socket gets a task immediately. The server does not first acquire a global connection permit, and there is no per-source ceiling. One source, or a distributed group of sources, can therefore consume the listener’s available connection resources.

2. No TLS handshake timeout

The TLS accept future can wait indefinitely for a ClientHello or later handshake bytes. Without a deadline, slow or silent peers retain resources until network cleanup, process termination, or some external component closes the connection.

3. Shutdown is observed too late

The service checks its stop condition only after a successful handshake. Pending handshakes do not promptly react to graceful shutdown, so stalled tasks may remain alive while the rest of the node is trying to stop.

Security impact

The confirmed impact is availability loss rather than confidentiality or transaction-integrity compromise. Once descriptors or task capacity are exhausted, legitimate TLS RPC clients cannot connect. Repeated accept errors may terminate the RPC task and can potentially propagate into broader node shutdown.

The attack is relatively cheap because the client does not need to perform a valid TLS exchange or submit a syntactically correct RPC request. It only needs network reachability and enough simultaneous TCP connections.

Several deployment choices reduce exposure. A loopback-only listener, a strict firewall, or a front proxy with connection and handshake limits can make the endpoint unreachable or bounded. Only deployments using the TLS RPC path are affected.

Safe validation approach

Testing should be performed only against an isolated TLS-enabled node. Open a bounded number of test TCP connections without sending TLS bytes, hold them longer than the intended handshake deadline, and verify that the server closes them automatically. Then confirm that a legitimate TLS RPC request still succeeds while the connection limit is under pressure.

The purpose of the test is to validate resource boundaries, not to exhaust the host. Monitoring should include open file descriptors, active handshake tasks, accepted connections, timeout counts, and RPC availability.

Remediation

Every TLS handshake should run inside a short timeout:

A timeout alone is not sufficient because attackers can continue opening new connections. The listener should acquire a global semaphore permit before spawning connection work and apply stricter per-source limits where practical. If no permit is available, it should reject or close the socket immediately.

Shutdown handling should race against the handshake so pending work is cancelled promptly:

The accept loop should treat EMFILE and temporary accept failures as overload conditions. Bounded backoff, alerting, and controlled recovery are preferable to terminating the entire RPC task. Operationally, an external TLS terminator with handshake deadlines and connection quotas can provide an immediate boundary while application changes are prepared.

Regression tests

The fix should be protected by tests that verify:

  1. Silent TCP connections are closed after the configured TLS handshake deadline.
  2. Connections beyond the global limit are rejected deterministically.
  3. Per-source limits prevent one client address from occupying the full budget.
  4. A valid TLS RPC request succeeds while the listener is under connection pressure.
  5. Graceful shutdown promptly cancels pending handshake tasks.
  6. Temporary accept failures use bounded backoff without bringing down the node.

Takeaway

Connection admission is part of an RPC service’s security boundary. Authentication cannot protect resources allocated before authentication begins, and request rate limits cannot govern clients that never finish becoming requests.

For Zakura operators, the immediate response is to keep TLS RPC behind a firewall or a properly configured TLS proxy with handshake deadlines and connection limits. For maintainers, the durable fix combines handshake timeouts, global and per-source admission controls, shutdown-aware cancellation, and resilient accept-error handling.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-tls-rpc-handshake-exhaustion/report.pdf

entry.title: Unauthenticated Zakura RPC Exposure Can Exhaust Node Resources
entry.content:
Zakura 1.2.0 can expose administrative RPC methods to unauthenticated remote callers when two settings are combined: the RPC listener is bound beyond loopback, and cookie authentication is disabled. In that deployment, an attacker who can reach the RPC port can request expensive history scans and large address collections without credentials.

The requests can consume node CPU, memory, and disk I/O. Repeated or concurrent calls can compete with peer synchronization, state management, and mempool processing, degrading RPC responsiveness and potentially making the node unavailable.

This is a configuration-dependent resource-exhaustion issue. Default installations are substantially safer because cookie authentication is enabled and the listener is restricted to loopback.

Vulnerability at a glance

The report identifies the affected product and version as:

  • Product: Zakura / zakurad
  • Version: 1.2.0
  • Status: published
  • Weakness classes: CWE-400, uncontrolled resource consumption; CWE-770, allocation of resources without limits or throttling; and CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function

The dangerous configuration has four requirements:

  1. RPC listens on a non-loopback address.
  2. Cookie authentication is disabled.
  3. The attacker can reach the RPC port.
  4. The attacker submits very large scan ranges or address collections.

When all four conditions are met, administrative methods become anonymous high-cost work queues.

What normal behavior should look like

Administrative RPC should be authenticated and available only to trusted networks. Expensive methods should also enforce explicit bounds on the requested range, number of addresses, result size, and concurrency.

The abnormal behavior is the inverse: a caller can request work far larger than the request itself suggests, and multiple requests can run at the same time against the same node resources. A small JSON-RPC request can therefore trigger a full-chain scan or collect a very large result set.

The call chain

The exposure begins during RPC setup. Authentication middleware is loaded only when enable_cookie_auth is true. If it is false, the server does not add the cookie-auth layer. Configuration validation does not reject the combination of a non-loopback listener and disabled authentication.

The resulting path is:

The issue is not limited to one method. getnetworksolps accepts an extremely large positive num_blocks value, while address-oriented methods accept large collections and ranges without practical item, span, pagination, or result-size limits.

Root causes

1. A high-risk configuration is accepted

The authentication middleware is conditional:

Disabling cookie authentication removes the protection, but the configuration does not reject or strongly warn when RPC is simultaneously bound to a non-loopback address. This turns an administrative interface into a remotely reachable anonymous endpoint.

2. History scanning has no practical upper bound

getnetworksolps converts a large positive num_blocks value into a traversal count. The value is not clamped to a documented safe window before the node walks its history:

Even if a request is small on the wire, the resulting backend work can be large.

3. Address queries collect too much at once

Address vectors, height spans, and returned rows are not governed by one resource budget or pagination contract. A range query can therefore scan a broad interval and collect all matching results in memory:

Without caps on address count, height span, result size, and concurrent calls, the cost scales with chain and index size.

Reproduction outline

The report used an isolated test environment with a non-loopback listener and cookie authentication disabled. The minimal validation pattern is to compare bounded requests with requests containing an extremely large block count and large address arrays while measuring duration and resource use.

Representative JSON-RPC shapes include:

These examples should only be evaluated against an isolated test node. The important security conclusion is not a particular request value, but that the server accepts unbounded work from an unauthenticated network caller.

Impact and limitations

Sustained requests can degrade RPC responsiveness and compete with synchronization, peer, and mempool work. Because the RPC process shares host resources with core node services, the operational impact depends on chain size, index size, storage speed, available memory, and request concurrency.

The issue does not by itself demonstrate fund theft or consensus corruption. It is primarily an availability and resource-isolation problem. Several factors reduce risk: cookie authentication is enabled by default, loopback binding blocks anonymous remote access, and network firewalls or an authenticated reverse proxy can prevent reachability.

The separate sendrawtransaction retry-channel issue mentioned in the source report is outside the scope of this analysis.

Remediation

The safest short-term deployment posture is to keep RPC on loopback or an authenticated private network. Do not disable cookie authentication on a listener reachable by untrusted clients. A reverse proxy can add network-level access control while a code fix is prepared, but it should not be treated as a substitute for application-level authentication.

Longer-term fixes should include:

  • reject startup when RPC is non-loopback and authentication is disabled, or require an explicit high-risk override;
  • clamp num_blocks to a documented safe maximum and return a controlled error for oversized values;
  • limit address count, height span, result size, and concurrent expensive requests;
  • paginate large result sets instead of collecting them without a bound; and
  • update configuration examples to show the safe authenticated deployment.

Regression tests should verify every listener and authentication combination, including IPv4 and IPv6 wildcard addresses. They should also confirm that huge num_blocks values fail quickly, address queries enforce count and range limits, result sizes are bounded, and bounded RPC calls remain responsive while peer synchronization and mempool processing continue.

Takeaway

Authentication and resource limits solve different problems, and an administrative API needs both. Zakura’s default settings provide meaningful protection, but accepting a remotely exposed listener with authentication disabled creates a direct path from an anonymous request to expensive backend work.

For operators, the immediate control is simple: bind RPC to loopback or a trusted private network and keep cookie authentication enabled. For maintainers, startup validation, strict work budgets, pagination, and concurrency controls should make the dangerous configuration and the expensive methods difficult to misuse.

Attachments

  • Original report: /attachments/zakura-rpc-resource-exhaustion/report.pdf

entry.title: How Zebra's Mempool Crawler Bypasses the Per-Peer Download Limit
entry.content:
Zebra limits concurrent transaction downloads to protect its mempool. The global limit is 500 slots, and the normal per-peer limit is five. A flaw in the mempool crawler path allows one ordinary P2P peer to bypass the per-peer limit and fill all 500 global slots with fake transaction IDs.

The node does not crash, and CPU and memory usage can remain normal. The failure is quieter: legitimate transactions are rejected with FullQueue, so transfers may remain unconfirmed, merchants may not receive payment confirmations, and miners may build templates without transactions that would otherwise be available.

The issue affects zebrad v6.3.0 and was also reproduced against historical versions 6.2.2 and 6.2.3. The report states that zcashd is not affected.

The intended protection

Zebra’s download pipeline has two relevant quotas:

The global limit prevents download and validation work from exhausting host resources. The per-peer limit prevents one peer from occupying the entire global pool. It was introduced to address an earlier class of transaction-download abuse.

The protection depends on the download request carrying the address of the peer that supplied the transaction. When that source is present, Zebra can count pending downloads for that peer and return FullQueue after the fifth item.

Where the crawler differs

The normal broadcast path preserves the source peer:

The crawler path is different. Zebra proactively asks a selected peer for its mempool transaction list. The response is queued with source=None, even though the crawler knows which connection supplied the response:

The if let Some(source) guard means that no per-peer accounting occurs when the source is None. A single crawler response can therefore inject thousands of IDs, while the global pool admits the first 500. Every later legitimate transaction encounters a full queue until slots are released.

Attack timeline

The attack only requires an ordinary P2P connection. No account, special privilege, or mining power is needed.

In the reported reproduction, the crawler selects three peers at random approximately every 73 seconds. When it selects the attacker’s connection, the attacker responds to the mempool request with about 5,000 fake transaction IDs and does not complete the subsequent getdata requests.

The resulting sequence is:

  1. The crawler selects the attacker’s peer.
  2. The attacker returns thousands of fake transaction IDs.
  3. The crawler queues the IDs without a source peer.
  4. All 500 global download slots become occupied.
  5. Legitimate transactions receive FullQueue and cannot enter the mempool.
  6. Download timeouts release slots after roughly 20 seconds.
  7. The next crawler cycle can fill the slots again.

With a single IP, selection is probabilistic and the disruption is intermittent. Because the default max_connections_per_ip is one, multiple cooperating IP addresses increase the attacker’s coverage. The report estimates that approximately 15 IPs can approach nearly continuous selection, although this is not a one-request permanent outage.

Why previous fixes do not close this path

The crawler bypass remains after two related hardening changes. One fix limits per-peer work when a source peer is present. Another charges actively pushed full transactions or transaction messages against the per-peer budget. Both protections work on paths that pass Some(peer).

The crawler explicitly passes None, so the guard bypasses both the accounting and the associated overload behavior. The code also treats crawler traffic as an intentional exemption without adding a compensating total limit for each crawler response or cycle.

That design creates a mismatch: the global pool is bounded at 500, but a single crawler response can attempt to populate the entire pool. A peer that repeatedly refuses the resulting getdata requests is not necessarily marked as misbehaving, and the crawler path does not consistently surface FullQueue as an overload signal.

Observed impact

The report reproduced the issue in an isolated Regtest environment with Zebra v6.3.0. During saturation:

  • mempool_currently_queued_transactions reached 500;
  • the per-peer full-queue metric did not appear, consistent with the skipped source check;
  • the fake peer log showed 5,000 returned transaction IDs; and
  • Zebra remained alive with stable memory and approximately 0.1-0.2% CPU.

This is an availability vulnerability, not a memory-exhaustion crash. It does not directly steal funds, alter existing blocks, corrupt on-disk state, or change consensus. The practical damage is transaction propagation failure and delayed confirmation.

The impact can reach multiple user groups. Wallet users may see transfers appear to vanish, merchants and payment gateways may wait indefinitely for confirmations, exchanges may experience delayed deposits and withdrawals, and miners may omit fee-paying transactions from block templates. Attacking several nodes at once could turn local transaction delays into broader propagation problems.

Recommended remediation

The crawler should preserve the source peer when it queues transaction IDs. The peer address is already known because the crawler initiated the connection, so the request should carry Some(peer) into download_if_needed_and_verify. This makes the existing per-peer cap apply naturally.

Additional defenses should make the crawler safe even if source tracking fails again:

  • impose a separate, substantially smaller transaction enqueue budget per crawler response and cycle;
  • associate repeated failed downloads with the supplying peer and apply misbehavior scoring or bans;
  • propagate FullQueue through the crawler path and disconnect peers that repeatedly inject unusable transaction IDs; and
  • remove or narrow the explicit crawler exemption instead of relying on a design comment as a security boundary.

Regression tests should cover both the ordinary and crawler paths:

  1. Confirm that the existing broadcast path still enforces the five-transaction per-peer limit.
  2. Return more than 500 fake transaction IDs from a crawler response and verify that one peer cannot occupy more than the configured per-peer quota.
  3. Verify that the per-peer counter records crawler downloads under the supplying peer.
  4. Confirm that a peer refusing getdata is assigned misbehavior and can eventually be banned.
  5. After saturation recovers, verify that legitimate transactions enter the mempool normally.

Takeaway

Resource limits are only effective when every path that consumes the resource carries the identity and accounting context used by the limit. Zebra’s normal transaction path preserves that context; the crawler path discards it. The result is a bounded but meaningful denial of service in which the node looks healthy while refusing the transactions its users need.

For operators, keeping peers and node versions monitored remains important, but configuration alone cannot reliably eliminate this code-path issue. For maintainers, preserving the source peer and adding crawler-specific budgets and overload handling are the key repairs.

Preview

  • Github repository: https://github.com/MemeshortFun/zcash/tree/main/zebra-mempool-crawler-slot-bypass

entry.title: Unauthenticated Memory Exhaustion in Zebra's Tracing Filter Endpoint
entry.content:
Zebra’s tracing configuration endpoint can become a remote denial-of-service primitive when it is exposed beyond a trusted local interface. An unauthenticated attacker can submit an oversized POST /filter request, causing the node to hold and parse the request body in memory. In testing, a 38 MB request grew the zebrad process to roughly 1,981 MB before the operating system’s out-of-memory killer terminated it.

The issue is configuration-dependent, but the impact is serious for an affected deployment: the node can become unavailable, and other services sharing the same host may also be killed or destabilized.

What the endpoint does

The /filter endpoint is part of Zebra’s tracing and filter-reload functionality. It is not enabled in a default installation. The relevant attack surface appears when Zebra is built with the filter-reload feature and tracing.endpoint_addr is configured to an address reachable by an attacker.

In the affected implementation, read_filter() in zebrad/src/components/tracing/endpoint.rs reads a POST /filter body with collect().await. There is no effective request-body size limit before the complete body is held in memory. The body is then parsed as a filter string, which adds another layer of allocation and produces an observed memory amplification of approximately 12x.

Attack path

The attack requires no credentials and can be carried out with an ordinary HTTP request:

  1. Connect to the externally reachable tracing endpoint.
  2. Send a large body to POST /filter.
  3. Let Zebra collect and parse the entire request in memory.
  4. Continue sending requests or use a sufficiently large body until the host reaches memory pressure.
  5. The operating system’s OOM killer terminates zebrad, and possibly other processes on the host.

The report’s test environment used Zebra v6.3.0 with filter-reload enabled. A 38 MB request increased resident memory to approximately 1,981 MB, after which the connection was interrupted and the process disappeared. A restart does not remove the exposure: while the endpoint remains reachable, the same request can be sent again.

A second security problem: unauthenticated writes

The endpoint is not limited to oversized reads. Unauthenticated users can also change logging filters through POST /filter. For example, an attacker can set filters such as zebrad=trace or zebra_network=trace without a token or login.

That capability is independently problematic. Trace-level logging can consume substantial CPU, disk, and memory, while also diluting useful audit records. It can therefore serve as a preparatory step before the memory-exhaustion request, increasing pressure on the host and making incident analysis harder.

Conditions that limit or increase the risk

Default installations are generally unaffected because the feature is not enabled and the endpoint is not configured. Binding the endpoint to a local-only address, such as 127.0.0.1, also prevents a direct remote connection.

The risk increases when:

  • Zebra is compiled with --features filter-reload;
  • tracing.endpoint_addr binds to an externally reachable address and port;
  • the endpoint is exposed without authentication or authorization;
  • there is no request-size limit or process-level memory cap; and
  • unrelated services share the same host.

The vulnerability is primarily an availability issue. The report does not demonstrate theft of funds, disclosure of confidential data, or manipulation of blockchain consensus. However, the OOM killer chooses which process to terminate, so the blast radius can extend to databases, wallets, monitoring agents, or other co-hosted services.

Recommended remediation

The most direct fix is to reject oversized request bodies before they are fully buffered. A hard Content-Length check should be combined with a streaming limit while reading, returning HTTP 413 Payload Too Large when the limit is exceeded. Relying on Content-Length alone is insufficient because clients can omit it or use a streaming transfer mode.

The endpoint should also require authentication and authorization. Binding it to loopback by default is a useful deployment safeguard, but it should not replace access control when remote administration is genuinely required. The filter string itself needs a length limit and validation as well.

Operational defenses can reduce the blast radius while code fixes are being prepared:

  • keep the endpoint off public interfaces;
  • place it behind an authenticated reverse proxy when remote access is necessary;
  • apply a cgroup or systemd memory limit to zebrad; and
  • monitor for unexpected filter changes, large POST bodies, and OOM-killer events.

Regression tests should verify that oversized bodies are rejected while the process remains alive, unauthenticated requests cannot read or change filters, and valid authenticated filter updates continue to work.

Takeaway

This incident illustrates why operational endpoints deserve the same security review as public APIs. A feature intended to make tracing convenient combines three dangerous properties when misconfigured: unauthenticated access, unrestricted request buffering, and the ability to increase logging verbosity. The result is a simple remote path to node termination.

For Zebra operators, the immediate action is straightforward: do not expose the tracing endpoint to untrusted networks. For maintainers, bounded streaming reads, authentication, input validation, and regression coverage should make the endpoint’s resource usage and trust assumptions explicit.

  • Github repository: https://github.com/MemeshortFun/zcash/tree/main/zebra-filter-memory-exhaustion

entry.title: How a Single RPC Call Can Crash a Zebra Node
entry.content:
Zebra is designed to keep its chain state predictable, but the report in this package shows how a single invalidateblock request can push that state into an impossible corner. The result is not data theft or consensus corruption. It is simpler, and in some ways more brutal: a remote caller can force the node to terminate.

What happened

The vulnerability appears when the only non-finalized chain is invalidated at its root. In that path, Zebra removes the entire chain from its internal chain_set. That would be fine if the rest of the system handled an empty non-finalized state as a normal condition. It does not.

Later, the write worker assumes a best chain still exists and calls expect() on the result of best_chain(). Once the state is empty, that assumption collapses and the process panics. Because the release build uses panic = "abort", the panic brings down the whole node.

Why it matters

This is a clean availability bug:

  • one request is enough to trigger it;
  • the request can be repeated after restart;
  • the RPC response may still look successful before the crash;
  • the impact is service loss, not a consensus fork or data leak.

That makes the issue especially painful for deployments that expose RPC on an untrusted network, including the official Lightwalletd Docker example described in the report.

Root cause in plain English

Two assumptions collide:

  1. invalidateblock is allowed to delete the only remaining non-finalized chain.
  2. update_latest_chain_channels() assumes there is always at least one non-finalized chain.

Those assumptions are individually understandable, but together they form a trap. An external RPC request can create the exact state that internal code claims should never happen.

Reproduction path

The report describes a minimal sequence:

  1. Create a state with only one non-finalized chain.
  2. Fetch the root block hash.
  3. Call invalidateblock(root_hash).
  4. Receive a normal-looking RPC response.
  5. The write worker panics while updating chain channels.
  6. The node exits.

The key detail is that the target must be the root of the only current non-finalized chain, not just any block at height 1.

Practical fixes

The report recommends three sensible defenses:

  • reject invalidations that would remove the last non-finalized chain, or support an explicit empty state;
  • stop using expect() on state that external input can invalidate;
  • only update chain channels after a successful invalidation and a confirmed best chain.

Operationally, the safest deployment posture is still the boring one: keep RPC behind authentication, bind exposed services to trusted interfaces, and avoid anonymous access on public networks.

Final note

This is a good reminder that crash bugs often come from small mismatches between internal invariants and external APIs. The API says “invalidate this block.” The internals say “this state can never be empty.” Security problems live in that gap.
